t: You shut a door at night while I look for dry ground.
I saw you leave your bed this morning. I had no bed to leave.
The rain sounds different when it lands on somebody else's roof.
You complain about a draft. I would welcome walls around mine.
One of us slept indoors. Guess which one is tired of hearing excuses.
I am done pretending your comfort and my cold are unrelated.
The god placed a roof above you. What duty came with that gift?
You thank the god for shelter while stepping past people without it.
Maybe your roof is a blessing. I wonder what that makes my night.
I almost believe shelter means favour. Then I look at who lacks it.
People built your roof. People can explain why I have none.
Do not call your good fortune divine while I sleep in mud.
You have been staring at my door all morning. Say what you mean.
I did not put you outside, whatever that look says.
My roof does not become larger because you resent it.
Ask me for help plainly. I will not answer silent blame.
I know where you slept. I do not know why you blame me.
You speak as though I chose every bed in this village.
The god gave me shelter. I never asked that you be denied it.
I thank the god for my roof and pray for yours. Is that wrong?
Maybe fortune chose badly. I still did not make the choice.
I have wondered why I am inside and you are not.
Builders made this roof. Take your complaint to whoever directs them.
A roof is timber and work, not proof that heaven prefers me.
You did not put me outside. You simply stopped noticing I was there.
Your doorway has room for sympathy, if nothing else.
I asked plainly before. You answered by changing the subject.
I am not asking you to stretch the walls with your hands.
Then stand beside me when I ask why the building has stopped.
You cannot choose every bed. You can choose whether this matters.
A blessing kept only for yourself begins to look like selfishness.
The god sees the fire inside and the person outside it.
Perhaps nobody chose this. Somebody still has to change it.
I do not know why fortune split us. I know which side is colder.
Good. Leave heaven aside and help me question the building order.
No prayer laid those beams. Work did, and more work can follow.
You accuse me of indifference because I cannot offer what I lack.
I saw you outside. I also saw every sleeping place already taken.
I can speak for another roof. I cannot promise when it rises.
Being indoors does not give me command over the builders.
I did not know you had asked me before. I know now.
I will listen. Stop speaking as if my bed was stolen from yours.
The god gave shelter through many hands. I will add mine where possible.
I can pray beside you and ask the builders what remains.
Maybe I called my roof providence because gratitude was easier than guilt.
I cannot explain the difference. I can admit it is unjust.
Exactly. People placed the beds. People can decide what comes next.
Blame poor planning before blaming somebody who happened to get a room.
You keep defending the walls while I keep waking wet.
I am tired of asking sheltered people to imagine the weather.
If you truly noticed, stop explaining and stand with me.
Another night outside will not make me easier to speak with.
Find me when you have help instead of reasons.
Perhaps you are only the nearest person with a door.
The god will hear me outside whether the housed do or not.
Keep the blessing if you must. The god will know how you used it.
Maybe I am angry at chance and giving it your face.
I want shelter more than I want an answer about providence.
The sky is not judging me. The village is simply failing me.
Save the blessing talk. Show me where the next beam goes.
I cannot tear down my roof to make this fair.
You want me ashamed when what you need is another building.
I offered my voice. I will not accept blame for every missing bed.
I see the unfairness. I resent being treated as its architect.
Keep shouting at my door. It will remain the same size.
I should have spoken sooner. That much belongs to me.
The god sheltered me. I can use that shelter to help others.
I will pray and work for another roof. I will not apologise for mine.
Perhaps my gratitude kept me from examining your need.
I do not know why I sleep inside. I know this anger builds nothing.
If you want fairness, challenge the order of construction.
The god did not choose my bed. The village did.
I am leaving before another cold night speaks through me.
Keep your reasons. I need to find somewhere dry.
I should not blame you for every wall. I still blame your silence.
Remember this conversation when you close your door tonight.
Do not follow me unless you know where I can sleep.
I spoke harshly. The cold remains, but those words were mine.
I will ask at the shrine and stop asking at your door.
The god will decide whether shelter excused that answer.
Perhaps nobody intended this. I still need distance from you.
I need sleep before I decide whether I owe an apology.
I will ask builders instead of heaven. At least they answer plainly.
There is no divine meaning here worth discussing. I need a roof.
I will speak for another roof. That is what I can offer.
I am sorry you slept outside. I am not sorry I slept indoors.
Find me tomorrow. We can ask what the next building needs.
I have heard enough blame for one doorway. I am leaving.
Next time I see you outside, I will not look away.
You deserve shelter. You did not deserve to accuse me of denying it.
I will pray that another roof rises soon. That is sincere.
May the god shelter you and soften both our words.
I may owe more than sympathy. Let me think what I can do.
I was sheltered and defensive. Both can be true.
Find whoever orders the work. I will stand there with you.
I will help seek shelter. I will not call the difference divine.
